metadata.title: The Policy Impact of PISA: An Exploration of the Normative Effects of International Benchmarking in School System Performance

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This OECD report is based on an expert questionnaire administered to members of the PISA Governing Board (PGB) representatives from PISA 2009 participating countries/economies, not on student microdata from PISA. The study therefore does not involve complex survey weighting of student responses (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) or replicate-weight procedures (e.g., BRR/jackknife) typical of ILSA achievement analyses. The analytic sample consists of 37 responding education systems (with separate responses for Belgium’s French/Flemish communities and the UK education systems), and the key outputs are descriptive judgments (e.g., perceived influence of PISA) and constructed indices (e.g., breadth of policy impact). As a result, weighting is not applicable in the sense used for PISA achievement scaling; interpretation should focus on representativeness limitations arising from one respondent per system and subjective ratings.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values (PVs) are not applicable because the study does not analyze cognitive achievement outcomes from PISA student assessments; instead, it uses an expert questionnaire about policy use of PISA. Missing-data handling for PV-based achievement scores is therefore not part of the methodology. The report’s limitations relate to questionnaire response completeness and subjective judgments rather than PV imputation or deletion rules.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The study used an expert questionnaire completed by PISA Governing Board (PGB) representatives from countries/economies that participated in PISA 2009. The analytic sample includes 37 responding education systems; responses from Uruguay and Brazil were received but excluded from the final analysis due to incomplete responses. Separate responses were analyzed and reported separately for Belgium’s French and Flemish Communities and for the English, Scottish, and Welsh education systems of the United Kingdom. The report also notes that the results draw on only one respondent per country/economy (with some systems contributing multiple individuals to the final response), and that all 37 respondents completed the multiple-choice items while extended-response item completeness varied across systems.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD report examines the normative impact of PISA on national/federal education policy-making using an expert questionnaire administered in July 2011 to PISA Governing Board representatives from 65 PISA 2009 participating countries/economies. The study collects perceptions of PISA influence (e.g., “very/moderately/extremely influential”), identifies which PISA result aspects (reading, mathematics, science, trends, equity, and attitudes) inspired policy or practice changes, and constructs a breadth-of-policy-impact index using “Yes/Partly/No” responses. It further reports how PISA is used in assessment and evaluation systems, curriculum standards, and performance targets, including examples of policy transfer and benchmarking. The report does not estimate student achievement models and therefore does not use PV-based scaling or ML prediction; instead, it provides descriptive cross-national evidence of policy uptake. Key limitations include one respondent per system, subjective judgments, and incomplete extended responses, which constrain the depth of country-specific examples.
